extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, craftsmen, patrons, and general readers interested in art and architectural aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for evaluating and producing architecture and allied crafts (especially Gothic/medieval-minded aesthetics), emphasizing the moral, social, and artistic consequences of workmanship, invention, finish, and variety. Useful for critics, designers, patrons, and teachers of design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudeness/Savageness as a noble character
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudeness or savageness (roughness of thought and roughness of work) is not degradation but a noble and essential character of Gothic (and certain other) architecture; it expresses the origin among Northern nations and can be an index of religious principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and value 'uncouth animation' and 'rough strength' produced by workmen who lack delicate finish; do not interpret ungainly shape or rigid limb as shameful — these are often the expression of a powerful spirit. Anti-pattern: mocking or refusing these qualities as mere ignorance or ugliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three systems of architectural ornament: Servile, Constitutional, Revolutionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural ornament may be classified into: (1) Servile ornament — execution or power of inferior workmen entirely subjected to the intellect of the higher; (2) Constitutional ornament — executive inferior power partly emancipated with a will of its own while obeying higher powers; (3) Revolutionary ornament — no executive inferiority is admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the taxonomy to judge the relation between designer and workman. Examples: Greek, Ninevite, Egyptian as principal servile schools but with differences (Greek gives lower worker subjects he can perfectly execute; Assyrian/Egyptian lower the method to a legal standard). This classification helps assess whether ornament is manufacture or art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian system: recognize individual value and accept imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: In the medieval/Christian system of ornament the 'slavery' of inferior workmen is done away with; Christianity recognizes the individual value of every soul and the worth of confessing imperfection, allowing fragments full of imperfection to be used indulgently to raise a noble whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the Christian injunction: 'Do what you can, and confess frankly what you are unable to do.' Value contribution from lesser minds and accept their imperfections as part of a larger, dignified composition rather than discarding them for perfect uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always look for invention first, execution second
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary merit is invention (thought/design); execution should help invention and be only as perfect as the inventor can accomplish without painful effort — 'Always look for invention first, and after that, for such execution as will help the invention, and as the inventor is capable of without painful effort, and no more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize creative originality over mechanical finish. Anti-patterns: demanding finish where there is no thought (''slaves' work, unredeemed'') or valuing mere technical neatness above imaginative design. Example contrast: Venetian glass (varied invention) vs English glass (perfect finish but manufactured sameness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Never encourage manufacture of unnecessary articles lacking invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not encourage the manufacture of any article not absolutely necessary, in the production of which invention has no share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a purchasing and patronage principle: avoid supporting trades that employ human labor in purely repetitive, thoughtless tasks (example: glass beads); support goods where invention or design contributes to human improvement (example: well-designed glass vessels, engraved vases, enamel-work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Never demand an exact finish for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not demand exact finish except when it serves a practical or noble end; exact finish for its own sake turns workers into machines and is morally and artistically wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept roughness when the thought requires it (e.g., a peasant's rough expression) and reserve delicate finish for masters whose finish furthers their noble purpose. Anti-pattern: insisting on 'polish' where it destroys the worker's thought or makes the work sterile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never encourage imitation or copying except for record-preserving
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not encourage imitation or copying of any kind, except for the sake of preserving record of great works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage mass copying that turns art into manufacture. Use copying only where archival or pedagogical preservation of exemplary works is intended, not as a source of new art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer rough work with thought to smooth work without thought
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to accept roughness and error that accompany a worker's thought than to insist on smooth accuracy produced without intellectual engagement; 'choose rough work than smooth work, so only that the practical purpose be answered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commissioning or judging work, favor pieces that demonstrate mental engagement even if they contain mistakes. Anti-pattern: preferring mechanically perfect but soulless products because they look neat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the rigid separation of thinker and worker
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not institutionalize a division in which one man always thinks and another always works; both thinker and worker should partake of both activities — 'the workman ought often to be thinking, and the thinker often to be working.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage masters to perform manual tasks (architect working in mason's yard; painter grinding colors) and workers to be given scope for imagination. Social aim: remove degradation of manual labor and make professions liberal by excellence rather than by social caste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection is essential to all great human work; perfection is a misunderstanding
rubrics_metrics.description: No noble work can be perfectly finished; the 'demand for perfection is always a sign of a misunderstanding of the ends of art.' Great minds are always beyond their powers of execution, and life itself implies imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge art with mercy toward imperfection as a sign of life and progress. Examples/arguments: Leonardo's pursuit of perfection led to unfinished works; natural asymmetry (foxglove blossom) is beautiful. Anti-pattern: treating absolute perfection as the criterion of artistic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changefulness/Variety is an essential element of Gothic spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety — the perpetual change of form and detail — is central to Gothic architecture; it arises from allowing independent operation to inferior workmen and is itself a reward of that freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value constructions that permit infinite variation (e.g., pointed arches with endless proportion variations, grouped shafts with many grouping possibilities). Anti-patterns: rigid standardization that produces monotony and reduces architecture to manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of repeated parts indicates degradation of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of degradation of the workman can be gauged by whether the parts of the building are alike; identical capitals and mouldings show complete degradation, whereas perpetual change indicates freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual inspection of repetition to infer the social/ethical conditions of production. If all parts are identical, suspect slave-like execution and absence of individual contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great art should not say the same thing repeatedly; it must be entertaining and novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Art (including architecture) must not simply repeat itself; 'the merit of architectural, as of every other art, consists in its saying new and different things' — repetition and monotony are not signs of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect architects to produce variety and interest as novel content akin to authors and painters; do not confuse 'love of order' (practical habit) with the creative unpredictability needed for art. Anti-pattern: demanding strict doctrinal forms (e.g., rigid 'orders') that prevent invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for products of 'healthy and ennobling labor'
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should demand and pay for products whose production 'brighten, strengthen, refine, or form' human beings rather than degrade them into mere machines; the moral character of production matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage consumer and civic choices that favour goods made under conditions that develop human intelligence and happiness. Policy implication: sacrifice some convenience/cheapness to promote ennobling labor conditions.
